name: Union of Concerned Scientists: food and farms (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the flood protection kept is for households in the US Upper Midwest.
summary: The Union of Concerned Scientists' Food and Environment programme ($4.5M in the year to September 2025, $5.1M with overhead) does analysis and advocacy on farms and food: wetlands and the farm bill's conservation rules, fertilizer, groundwater, farm trade and farmworkers. This model counts its one win of the year with a value at stake: its estimate that the Upper Midwest's wetlands avert about $23 billion of flood damage a year was part of the case for the federal wetland protections (Swampbuster) that a court upheld in May 2025 against a challenge filed in 2024; its other work is a share. At the defaults a dollar given keeps about 0.0005 years of healthy life per $1,000 (flood damage averted, valued as consumption to the average American), from 0.000008 to 0.025 on the combined range. It is low because the challenge was unlikely to succeed, the government and four other groups fought the case (UCS, not a party, is credited with 1%), only farmed wetlands are at stake and drain slowly, and the money kept goes to US households, where a dollar does far less than in poor countries. The result is mostly uncertainty: the share credited to UCS, the chance the challenge would have won and the drainage rate each move it several times. The one branch is discounted for missing data: nothing about the work's outcome is measured.

rows.label: Years a won reform counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The shared years a won reform counts ($win_years_counted): the protections kept count for the years before the question would have been settled anyway; the drainage builds up over them (wetland_share_lost).

rows.label: One year's discount factor
rows.explainer: The shared discount rate, as a factor per year.

rows.label: Average years of drainage built up over the years counted, discounted
rows.formula: (1 - (years_of_impact + 1) * year_discount_factor ^ years_of_impact + years_of_impact * year_discount_factor ^ (years_of_impact + 1)) / ((1 - year_discount_factor) * (1 - year_discount_factor)) / pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, years_of_impact)
rows.explainer: In year t of the years counted, t years' drainage is gone: the discounted sum of 1, 2, … over the years counted (an increasing annuity), over the discounted years themselves, so the build-up is weighted like the years it multiplies. About 2.9 at 5 years and 4%.

rows.label: Share of the wetlands Swampbuster protects (farmed land of farmers in USDA programmes)
rows.explainer: Swampbuster binds only farmers who take USDA programme benefits, on wetlands on or next to farmland; the region's other wetlands are forested, public or under state law (Minnesota's Wetland Conservation Act, Wisconsin's wetland rules). Nationally about a sixth of non-federal wetlands sit on cropland, pasture and conservation-reserve land and most on forest land (USDA's 1997 National Resources Inventory); the share is higher in the farmed prairie-pothole parts of the Upper Midwest (Iowa, the Dakotas, southern Minnesota) and lower in the forested north. 30% (15% to 50%), our judgment.

rows.label: Share of those wetlands drained a year if Swampbuster fell
rows.explainer: Before Swampbuster (1985) the US lost inland wetlands at about half a percent a year, mostly drained for farming (Fish and Wildlife Service, 1950s-1970s); with high crop prices and cheap tile drainage, farmers freed of the rule would drain at about that rate: 0.5% a year (0.2% to 1%), our judgment. With the farmed share, about 0.15% of the region's wetlands a year, below the pre-1985 national rate because most of the region's wetlands aren't farmed.

source.title: Frayer et al. (1983), Status and Trends of Wetlands and Deepwater Habitats in the Conterminous United States, 1950s to 1970s (US Fish and Wildlife Service)
source.note: Losses of palustrine (inland, mostly farmable) wetlands of about 4.5 million hectares (11 million acres) between the mid-1950s and mid-1970s: about half a million acres, some half a percent, a year, mostly to agriculture.

rows.label: Average share of the flood protection lost over the years counted if the protections fell
rows.explainer: Drainage builds up: the protected share × the yearly rate × the average years of drainage built up over the years counted (buildup_years, weighted like the discounted years). Wetlands' flood protection is taken as proportional to their area.

rows.label: Value of a dollar of flood damage averted to US households, in units of value
rows.explainer: A dollar of flood damage averted, valued like a dollar of consumption to the average American: one over the household survey's consumption per person (the Consumer Expenditure Survey, 2024, in 2025 dollars: the one scale for US public money, docs/normalization.md 2.14) in ln(consumption), × the shared value of doubling consumption, as the Federation of American Scientists' model values a dollar of US public good.

rows.label: Value kept per dollar of the yearly protection, in units of value
Chance the challenge would in the end have struck down the protections
rows.explainer: CTM Holdings v. USDA (filed 2024) argued that Swampbuster exceeds Congress's power and aimed for the Supreme Court. The reference class: every earlier challenge failed (Horn Farms v. Johanns, 7th Circuit 2005, upheld it under the spending power), but the Supreme Court has narrowed federal wetland power before (Sackett v. EPA, 2023). One event, so drawn as one: 10% (2% to 30%), our judgment.

rows.label: Years from the win until the policy takes effect
rows.explainer: Had the challenge won in the end, it would have been after appeals (a year or two), and drainage would follow: 2 (1 to 3) years, our judgment; discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the policy takes effect
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Discounted years of impact
rows.explainer: The years counted, discounted, after the wait.

rows.label: Flood protection kept over the years counted, in units of value (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The yearly protection × the share at stake × its value per dollar × the chance the challenge would have succeeded × the discounted years.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), a multiplier
rows.explainer: How far UCS's $23 billion can be trusted: one organisation's model of residential flood losses, not peer-reviewed evaluation, and flood protection may not fall in proportion to wetland area. 0.8 (0.5 to 1.0), our judgment. The drainage judgment's doubt is in its own ranges, not here.

rows.label: Share of that chance the 2025 ruling removed
rows.explainer: The district court's ruling (29 May 2025) is final: no appeal was filed by the July 2025 deadline. But it rested partly on the plaintiffs not exhausting USDA's own appeals, and the same backers could bring a new case, so the ruling removed most, not all, of the risk in the years counted: 0.9 (0.7 to 1.0), our judgment. Who else defended the rule (the government, four groups) is the credit share, not asked here.

source.title: Food & Water Watch (5 August 2025), on the final ruling in CTM Holdings v. USDA
source.quote: Pacific Legal Foundation could file a new case challenging Swampbuster in the future.
source.note: Also: "The decision not to appeal means that the district court decision is final and binding."

rows.label: UCS's share of the resources behind the defence
rows.explainer: The defence was the Justice Department's for USDA and the intervenors' (the Iowa Farmers Union, the Iowa Environmental Council, Dakota Rural Action and Food & Water Watch, represented by the Environmental Law & Policy Center); UCS was not a party, its flood figure is not in the intervenors' brief, and the court ruled on the spending power and on administrative exhaustion. Its analysis appears in the Iowa Environmental Council's account of the case and in UCS's claim that it 'helped defeat' the suit (annual report p. 15). One analysis against two years of litigation by the government and four groups: 1% (0.1% to 5%), our judgment.

rows.label: Other food and farm work, as a share of the modelled value
rows.explainer: The rest of the programme and the win's other goods, each a share of the wetland branch's value: fertilizer (nitrogen) analysis and advocacy, whose cuts in nitrous oxide and nitrate pollution would count in tonnes and health; the San Joaquin Valley groundwater recommendations; the farm bill's conservation programmes and farmworkers' heat and pesticide protections; analysis of the costs of tariffs to farmers; and, from the wetlands kept, nitrate removal, habitat, the carbon drainage would release, and Sodbuster's protection of erodible land (decided in the same case). The programme's other work has no counted win of the year, so it counts only for the chance it moves a later rule; the wetlands' other goods ride on the same small chance and credit as their flood protection: together half the wetland branch's value, 50% (15% to 60%), our judgment, inside the family's bounds.
